Living with leopards in the Himalayas. In the afternoon of Feb 22, 67-year-old Bulal Maharjan, a farmer on the outskirts of Kathmandu, was sitting on his porch chopping cauliflower leaves to feed his chickens. Hearing a loud thud as a parked motorcycle toppled, he turned and watched in horror as a leopard leapt away from the fallen vehicle and lunged at him, piercing its sharp canines into his forehead, its claws lacerating his hands. Within seconds, neighbours swarmed in, and the leopard ran into a nearby house. They eventually trapped the animal inside. After nearly two hours of panic that saw two more people injured trying to control the distressed big cat, forest division officials managed to sedate it and bring the situation under control. Maharjan still can’t shake off memories of the attack. “For three days straight, I couldn’t even sleep. Every time I began to doze, the scene of this attack would jolt me up!” he says. “I think we should just get rid of this animal. Period.” Conflicts with people are growing as expanded forest land and climate change push the creatures into human settlements Sentiments like Maharjan’s are common across Nepal, where leopards have been responsible for significant loss of human life and livestock. Research shows that from the years 2000 to 2020, conflicts between humans and four large mammals — elephants, rhinos, tigers and common leopards — claimed 887 human lives and led to the killing of 1,139 animals. Of these, common leopards were the leading cause of human deaths at an average of 19 deaths per year, and the species most frequently killed. To try to bring the conflict under control, Nepal and other countries with human-large predator conflicts are exploring a range of solutions. Nepal has three ecological zones: lowland dominated by Bengal tigers, mountainous regions where snow leopards roam free, and the vast mid-hill ruled by common leopards as the top predator. While protected areas in the lowlands and mountains receive dedicated conservation funding for their charismatic predators, the mid-hills are largely managed as community forests. The celebrated community forest program is a key reason for leopards’ thriving in the mid-hills. In the early 1990s, amid worsening floods and landslides linked to forest degradation, King Birendra handed over management of large swaths of forest to local communities so that they would have stakes in conservation, and benefit from timber and fruit harvests. Today, almost 47 per cent of Nepal is covered by forest patches. About a third of that area belongs to community forests, most of which are run by people living in the mid-hills. “But what the communities didn’t realise was they also restored habitats so that the top carnivores could return,” said Kedar Baral, a wildlife biologist for Nepal’s Bagmati province. In 2020, Baral’s team conducted an analysis of leopard scat collected in the mid-hills that showed that 27pc of the animals’ diet consisted of domestic animals, while the wild ungulates that big cats typically prefer to hunt, like barking deer and wild boars, made up only 10pc. In search of sprouting leaves, barking deer venture from the dense community forests to farmland, and “as the deer enter the farmlands, that’s where the leopard follows,” says Baral, bringing them into contact with domestic livestock. Nepal’s hydropower and construction projects are also expanding into remote forested areas at higher elevations, disturbing habitat and bringing workers as well as a new hunting pressure against top predators, including common leopards, living there. That forces the leopards and their prey to leave their territory, says Madhu Chetri, a wildlife ecologist at the National Trust for Nature Conservation. Climate change might be influencing conflict patterns, too. While he was working as a district forest officer in Nepal’s western mid-hills, Baral and his team were repeatedly called to respond to common leopard attacks on local communities. Over time, he noticed a change in the pattern: Conflict incidents and human or livestock deaths were increasingly reported from higher-elevation settlements. Reporting in 2023, Baral and colleagues investigated whether climate change was driving this shift. Using data from 343 sites across Nepal based on signs of leopard scat, animal tracks and kills, he modeled habitat preferences of leopards, considering factors such as temperature, rainfall and elevation. The results suggest that leopards prefer mid-hill conditions at around 1,000 meters with moderate temperatures and high rainfall. Warming climates are likely expanding the range of suitable habitat uphill, which could allow the leopard population to grow and, as a result, have a higher risk of conflict with humans. Of course, it is a conservation success to be celebrated when numbers of threatened or endangered large carnivores increase — whether they be lynx, wolves, tigers or leopards — but it also presents new challenges, says Philip Nyhus, a conservation biologist at Colby College in Maine. Solutions to the problem have two parts, he adds: first, to keep wildlife separate from people and their livestock to prevent conflict to begin with, and second, to mitigate impacts when conflicts do occur. “A lot of attention has been given to the second piece,” he says. “What would be better is if we could prevent conflict from happening in the first place.” There are international examples to draw from. In the Argentinian Dry Chaco forest, for example, small households in woody areas have faced frequent attacks by pumas on sheep and goats. Sofia Nanni, a conservation biologist at the National Scientific and Technical Research Council of Argentina, worked with locals to come up with the idea of trying spiked leather collars on livestock, an approach that had proved successful in reducing leopard attacks on cows in countries like Iran. “We found a local artisan who made collars for dogs and we asked him if he could make collars,” Nanni says. Tracking collared goats and sheep for two years, her team found that the puma predation in uncollared animal groups was 10 times higher than that in collared groups. Several other strategies are successfully reducing leopard and other top predator conflicts globally. Still, changing attitudes and implementing effective interventions, as well as better compensation, can take years, while frustration among affected communities continues to grow. Damage assessment. PRESIDENT Donald Trump’s approval rating has hit an all-time low according to the latest Economist/YouGov poll. The survey found 62 per cent of Americans disapprove of the president’s performance while 63pc say the country is headed in the wrong direction. These are Trump’s worst numbers since he returned to the White House last year. The results align with findings of other polls, which show he has fallen out of favour with the majority of Americans. The slide isn’t just about an unpopular war with Iran. Trump’s management of the economy is also driving public discontent. The first 18 months of the mercurial leader’s second term have been defined by disruption at home and abroad. His ‘America First’ unilateralism has meant military strikes on multiple countries and upending of the global trading system. It reflects contempt for international law and other nations’ sovereignty. For a president who promised to end wars, not start them, his record is the opposite. Trump assumed American power could browbeat other countries into compliance at no cost to the US. That was a miscalculation. His overreliance on force also failed to produce the results he wanted. Trump may be extreme in his imperious, unilateralist ways but there is continuity with past US conduct in an important respect. Throughout its history of dealing with other nations, the US has underestimated the power of nationalism and the resistance it would meet in trying to force its will on others. It found that in its interventions in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq, which entangled Washington in unwinnable wars, produced strategic blunders and doomed its military adventures. Today, it is finding that again in the war against Iran. Trump also doesn’t seem to understand that the unipolar world long passed into history. In today’s multipolar world, countries will not so easily bend to Washington’s will. Indeed, the more Trump makes blusterous claims and tweets about how he has the power to get what he wants, the more it exposes his inability to secure his goals. There is no shortage of commentary on Donald Trump’s personality and record. Two of the latest books are worth noting. Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan and Betrayed: America didn’t vote for this by Ira Shapiro and Anne Kim. Both cover the first year plus of Trump’s second presidency and deliver stinging indictments of his performance. Betrayed is written by a broad coalition of distinguished bipartisan experts from among former government officials, lawyers, scholars and journalists. They are members of what is called the Common Sense Coalition. They chronicle the damage Trump has done to his country and to America’s standing in the world. This damage assessment is undertaken across multiple areas — economy, foreign policy, democracy and free speech, judiciary, voting system, education and climate. The book’s main point is that Americans did not vote for what Trump is doing and the disorder he is producing. His abuses of power must be stopped and his team members held accountable if America’s crisis is to end. With his approval ratings having plunged Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes towards the US. Though brief the chapters are pointed. The one on a weaker America is especially sharp. It argues that Trump has fractured the foundations for global stability. His costly and impetuous military adventures without a strategy or respect for international law and his contempt for traditional allies have endangered US security. The authors describe an unchecked president dragging the country into multiple conflicts with scant regard for the fallout. The attack on Iran, they argue, lays bare the hallmarks of his foreign policy decision making — impulsiveness, prioritising force over diplomacy, failure to take rational decisions based on their likely impact and trashing the concerns of allies. They frame his National Security Strategy as a reversal of eight decades of US foreign policy. This has resulted in ‘America Weaker’ and ‘America Alone’ and drained its soft power. Its international stature has diminished. Trump has alienated virtually all allies who had helped the US maintain global peace. The authors also argue Trump has misused and politicised the military and packed it with yes-men afraid of telling him the truth. In the chapter on the rule of law the writers hold Trump guilty of violating limits on presidential power, threatening the integrity of courts and usurping Congressional powers. Core civil liberties have been threatened. He is seen as weaponising government machinery including the Justice Department to punish political opponents and suppress dissent. He has violated court orders and vilified judges while shielding his friends from legal accountability. Regime Change is no less scathing about Trump’s record in office. Its subtitle Inside the imperial presidency of Donald Trump indicates its focus is on the inner workings of the White House. It is a riveting, richly sourced account of the chaos wreaked by a president who has acted with impunity and radically changed the office he occupies. It narrates how efforts have been made to stop Trump but failed. Based on over 1,000 interviews, it takes the readers behind the scenes to offer insights into Trump’s decision-making that has been so consequential and of course harmful for the country. How his team fell in line with his decisions even when they strongly disagreed is exemplified by a telling exchange between Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu during his February visit to Washington when he convinced Trump to attack Iran. The Israeli leader assured Trump that regime change would succeed in Iran and its nuclear capability would be destroyed, before Tehran could seize the Strait of Hormuz. The CIA director rubbished this view while the secretary of state called it “farcical”. But Trump prevailed. Trump’s conduct has hardened global attitudes toward the US. Friends, allies and adversaries view the erratic swings in American policy with alarm. The latest poll by the Pew Research Centre captures the shift. China is viewed more favourably than the US in most countries surveyed. Given the turbulence of the past 18 months, that result is hardly unexpected. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

A hard state?. THESE days we are repeatedly told that the Pakistani state has been soft on anarchy for far too long. This is the considered and stated position of many state officials as well as of many supporters of those in power. Common people may hold any number of positions that one finds distasteful but the same sentiments being voiced by those in power invite both scrutiny and concern. For the last three years, there has been much chatter about turning Pakistan into a ‘hard state’. No one has given an adequate definition of what this entails, but based on disparate statements and impulses, we can gather this has something to do with protecting the rights of the state and the decision-makers who staff it. These rights are being obtained via a frequently violent trade-off with the rights of the people of Pakistan. The projected consequence of such a trade-off is that protest of all shades becomes a privilege. Demands can only be voiced with due approval through vetted content and NOCs. Speech is to be regulated via defamation, criminalisation laws, and an apparently pliant judiciary till it takes on an acceptable hue, or preferably till it becomes an echo of the state’s. These impulses are neither unique to the Pakistani state nor are they exceptional to this current moment. Trysts with authoritarianism dot the country’s past and arguably lie at the roots of its state structure. British viceregal authority bequeathed an overdeveloped administrative apparatus, which has since then done exceedingly well to reproduce itself and the privileges of those who staff it. When given a chance, politicians of nearly all stripes — centralists, federalists, provincial magnates, or constituency-level bigwigs — have been more than happy to fortify this arrangement for their own and their clients’ benefits. And yet there is a question that should gnaw at anyone who thinks about the trade-off at the table. What is all of this for? If people are being asked to voluntarily or otherwise forfeit their constitutional or social rights, it only makes sense to interrogate what end goal this forfeiture is designed to serve. Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Forfeiture of individual liberty is commanded by all states in service of some basic objectives. Usually the foremost of these objectives is territorial sanctity: no state tolerates geographic loss and will usually strip people of their rights, property and lives to prevent it. The Pakistani state is fairly typical in this manner. It deals with separatism/secessionism the way many other post-colonial states do, and with variable degrees of success. The bigger question on that front then is whether its strategy for preventing the rise or growth of this factor is useful at all. Beyond the protection of geographic boundaries, what other objectives do limits on individual liberty serve? Other states offer different types of answers. The case of China — paradigmatic for the 21st century — has a very simple one. It places limits on various forms of individual rights for the protection and promotion of the CCP’s endeavours. The main endeavour, since the 1970s at least, has been the growth and collective prosperity of the Chinese people via the unleashing of productive forces (labour and capital), both by the state and by private enterprise. The state under one-party rule decides the degree of this unleashing, its objectives, and ultimately the distribution of its fruits. In the previous century, socialist states decided that the true fulfilment of human life lay in getting rid of privatised forms of exploitation. And so a suspension of individual liberty was done in service of collective ownership of resources, commandeered by the state. Social democratic states in Western Europe decided to infringe on the rights of capital owners over their profit in order to redistribute benefits to the working class via taxation. The late-20th-century Asian Tigers took away social rights of the working poor to generate double-digit capitalist growth. There are other, less palatable answers too. The fascists in Germany stripped the rights, property, and lives of one minority group and various ideological dissenters (primarily the communists) in service of its ethnonationalist and expansionist agenda. At present, the ruling party in India targets individual liberties of specific segments, such as Muslims, to fulfil the cultural agenda of its majority base. In all of these examples, the use of state power is for some larger agenda; a larger agenda in the name of the public (or at least an important part of it), built on specific ideational values and postulates. Something being done in service of something bigger, grander, and to varying degrees, collective. So one must pose the question: what objective does this particular, three-year-old vintage of the ‘hard state’ serve in Pakistan? To date there is no coherent answer. We do not know what the killing of protesters — regardless of the agreeability of their demands — in AJK is going to achieve. What goal banning political movements in the peripheries serves. What Form-47ing election outcomes does. What the hollowing out of the opposition, judiciary, media or civil society helps obtain. If the answer is to maintain territorial integrity, then the vast majority of those whose rights stand stripped away carry no geographic ambitions. If the answer is to unleash GDP growth rates of the kind unseen in the last two decades, then one must reluctantly point out that the needle is yet to move up at all. If the answer is to project sovereignty and stature on the world stage at a time of global upheaval, the logical follow-up is a) whose stature and b) sovereignty in whose name? There are no ready grand answers at the end of this line of inquiry because there is likely no grand thought among those steering the ‘hardening’. The actual answers, if one were to hazard a guess, are probably several degrees more modest: the prolonging of duration in office, an improvement in personal quality of life, and the distribution of gifts and sinecures to a small coterie of loyalists at the expense of everyone else. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums. X: @umairjav Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

Farewell to arms?. PALESTINIAN resistance group Hamas recently made a major concession by agreeing to give up its weapons. It should be remembered that along with its political activities, the movement has an armed wing dedicated to the liberation of Palestine. The group’s weapons will be surrendered to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the Palestinian technocratic body formed under US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. In essence, Hamas has thrown the gauntlet to Israel: it is ready to surrender its weapons, but will the Zionist state end its occupation of Gaza? This remains the million-dollar question. Mr Trump was upbeat about the development, saying that Israel was “very happy” about it. However, while there had been no official reaction from Tel Aviv at the time of writing, most Israeli politicians, including some in the cabinet, have decried the move, calling for the destruction of Hamas. It will be interesting to see whether Israel honours its end of the deal and vacates occupied Palestinian territory in Gaza. Going by past precedent, the Israelis are not known for keeping their word. Also, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an election in October , and there is widespread anti-Palestinian sentiment amongst the electorate. But the Israeli leader may not want to annoy the American president by appearing to sabotage Mr Trump’s Gaza peace plan. Lest we forget, Israel has murdered over 73,000 Palestinians — more than 21,000 of them children — since the Oct 7, 2023 attacks, and while its killing spree has lessened in intensity, it has not stopped completely since the ceasefire came into effect last year. Moreover, the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains appalling. It should be kept in mind that Hamas and other Palestinian groups have continued their armed struggle against Israel because the Zionist state has closed all avenues of peacefully resolving the Palestine question. Almost the entire Israeli political class is opposed to a Palestinian state, illegal settlements continue to proliferate, and Gaza — which even before the 2023 attacks was virtually under siege — lies in ruins. Meanwhile, Israeli provocations against Al Aqsa have not stopped. If this situation is to change, there must be a clear pathway for a Palestinian state, an end to Israeli brutalities against the Arab population, and complete withdrawal from all occupied territories. Knowing the current political climate in Israel, this is asking for the moon. However, Mr Trump, who sees himself as a ‘peacemaker’, and his BoP must press Israel to at least start the process by withdrawing from Gaza, and allowing unimpeded humanitarian assistance into the Strip. If Tel Aviv does not leave Gaza, it will show the world that it is not serious about peace, and is committed to the occupation of Palestine and to the extermination of the Palestinian people. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

Criminal record verification of Lahore's commercial drivers in the offing. LAHORE: The city traffic police have initiated verification of the criminal record of 348,000 commercial vehicle drivers following reports that they were involved in 48 percent of the total fatal road crashes. The decision was taken during a high-level meeting, where official data pertaining to repeated crashes and unsafe driving history of commercial and public service vehicles was presented. Chaired by Chief Traffic Officer (CTO) Syed Abdul Raheem Shirazi, the meeting reviewed the growing trend of commercial vehicle-related crashes and formulated a strategy to address the underlying causes. SP Headquarters Fakhar Bashir Raja had been assigned a special mandate to conduct an in-depth analysis of crash patterns and recommend evidence-based interventions to prevent future fatalities. A traffic police spokesperson said that the meeting was informed that Lahore had approximately 8.2 million registered vehicles, including 348,000 commercial vehicles, representing nearly five percent of the city’s total registered vehicle fleet. Despite their relatively small share, he said, commercial vehicles were involved in 48 percent of fatal road crashes, underscoring the need for immediate regulatory and enforcement measures. Traffic police data shows commercial drivers involved in 48pc of all fatal road crashes The meeting passed directions to the relevant police officers for the verification of the criminal background, driving history, licence status, and overall eligibility of every commercial and public service vehicle driver. “Drivers with criminal records, a history of repeated traffic crashes, habitual traffic violations, or conduct posing a threat to public safety will not be granted permits or licences to operate commercial vehicles,” said CTO Sherazi. He said that transport unions and commercial vehicle owners had been instructed to ensure that no driver was employed or entrusted with a vehicle without proper background verification, including a valid character certificate and complete record clearance. The move would help bring down serious and fatal traffic crashes across the provincial capital, the CTO said and warned that vehicle owners and transport operators who knowingly employ or facilitate high-risk drivers would also be held accountable under the law. “Accountability will extend beyond negligent drivers to those who enable them. Owners who disregard safety standards by allowing unfit drivers to operate commercial vehicles will face strict legal action,” he said. The meeting also resolved to undertake verification of driving licences of all commercial and public service vehicle drivers and granted approval for strict enforcement action against individuals found operating vehicles with fake, forged, expired, suspended, or otherwise invalid driving licences. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

Justin Greaves steadies West Indies in second Test against Pakistan. Justin Greaves made an unbeaten 64 to steer West Indies to 239-5 at stumps on a rain-shortened opening day of the second and final Test against Pakistan in Trinidad on Sunday. After a match-winning display with the ball in the first Test last week, Greaves displayed what has now become his trademark ease and composure at the crease in a battling knock at Queen’s Park Oval. His only error of judgement came just after reaching the half-century mark when captain Babar Azam put down a straightforward chance at leg-slip off spinner Sajid Khan. Greaves at that time was almost hobbling after a left leg injury sustained while completing a sharp run that necessitated lengthy treatment on the field. His sixth-wicket partnership with Roston Chase (36 not out) was worth 66 runs at the close of play and Greaves will be hoping for a return to his usual athletic mobility when he resumes the innings with his captain on the second morning. He had come to the crease in mid-afternoon at 91 for three as Kavem Hodge became Khan’s first wicket. When Amir Jangoo fell to a leg-side catch to give debutant pacer Ubaid Shah his first Test wicket with the first ball of a new spell, Pakistan sensed the chance to break the back of the West Indies resistance. However Greaves and Shai Hope provided a measure of stability in a 53-run stand until seamer Mohammad Ali, the most impressive of the bowlers on the day, bowled Hope off the inside-edge for 29 to leave the innings in the balance at 173 for five. Pakistan omit Abbas Earlier, Pakistan’s bewildering decision-making — on and off the field of play — highlighted a rain-affected morning session. Mohammad Abbas, the tourists’ best bowler by some distance from the 90-run defeat in the first Test, was dropped despite a match haul of eight for 85, including five for 22 in the second innings. A second Pakistani debutant, Awais Zafar, got his chance due to the finger injury sustained by former captain Shan Masood while compiling a determined century in the first Test. Pakistan’s think-tank seemed convinced of the wisdom of playing an additional slow bowler on a surface devoid of grass, drafting in Khan as an off-spinning option alongside left-arm orthodox bowler Ali Usman, who went wicketless on debut in the first Test. Khan’s first notable act in the match was to take the catch at long-leg which sent Tagenarine Chanderpaul to the pavilion for 15 as he failed to control a hook shot off Mohammad Ali after a brisk opening stand of 49 with Brandon King. “We needed those partnerships at the end of the day and it was good to see those guys (Greaves, Hope and Chase) making those contributions,” said King in summing up the day’s effort. “It would be nice if we get more of the same from them tomorrow and Justin and Roston can go on to get hundreds.” As easily as the runs flowed, especially off King’s bat, in the early exchanges after Chase opted to bat first, both could have been dismissed earlier with more attacking tactics as they each benefited from edges at catchable height through the vacant third slip position. Mohammad Ali was even pleading with Babar for additional support in the slip cordon following the third of those fortunate escapes. King’s luck ran out though following the 90-minute rain break as Usman snared him for his first Test wicket, leg-before for 46.

Oil tumbles as Trump cancels attack on Iran to reach deal aimed at reopening Hormuz. Oil prices tumbled more than $4 a barrel on Monday after US President Donald Trump held off on a fresh attack on Iran, seeking to reach a quick deal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures slid $4.49, or 5.11 per cent, to $83.44 by 0408 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $79.77 a barrel, down $4.90, or 5.79pc. Both contracts jumped more than 20pc last month after fighting between the US and Iran resumed and as attacks on several tankers around Oman heightened security concerns, deterring shippers from entering the Gulf to load oil. In a sign of de-escalation, Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the vital strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. IG market analyst Tony Sycamore says, “The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the Strait, potentially through an attack on a U.S. base or a tanker transiting the waterway.” Two tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait out of the Red Sea over the weekend while traffic in the Strait of Hormuz slowed following reports of vessel attacks, shipping data showed on Monday. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday. On Sunday, Opec+ approved an oil production quota increase of around 188,000 barrels per day from September, the producer group said, in a move that completes the unwinding of a layer of voluntary output cuts. Due to export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstan caused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, successive monthly Opec+ hikes over most of this year have remained largely on paper with little impact on the market.

Missing weapon, forensic inconsistencies puzzle investigators in Raza ‘murder’ case. KARACHI: Police investigators probing the death of a 25-year-old former IBA student and aspiring businessman have found that Mir Raza Ali Khan was facing financial losses in his business, but they doubt the theory that he took his own life, even though the evidence collected so far points to suicide, it emerged on Sunday. They are, however, hopeful of “resolving the case within a very short time”. The aspiring businessman’s body, bearing a gunshot wound to his chest, was recovered from bushes near Shahi Qila in Gulistan-i-Jauhar, opposite the University of Karachi, two days after he went missing and was allegedly kidnapped from his home in PECHS, Block-2. One official familiar with the investigation so far told Dawn , on condition of anonymity, that certain things had emerged during the course of the investigation, prompting investigators to focus more on the possibility of suicide than murder. Detectives trace former IBA student and entrepreneur’s final movements; financial losses emerge as key focus in probe Elaborating, the official said that Raza, as usual, arrived at his home in PECHS, early in the morning after closing his shop at Bahadurabad Chowrangi. After some time, he went back to his shop/office, where he took a pistol and returned in his car. He left the keys to his car and house. He also left his watch and some cash for his mother. Inside the home, he deleted all the data from his iPhone. The official added that Raza hired an online cab and asked the driver to play his favourite song, according to the driver’s statement recorded by investigators. He paid the driver double the required fare. CCTV footage from the place where the driver dropped him off in Gulistan-i-Jauhar showed that he was “roaming” around, and no one else was seen accompanying him. After deleting all the data from his phone, he went offline. It has been established that he himself deleted the data. He may have thrown away his mobile phone, which was later picked up by someone from the place where his body was found. When the person inserted a SIM card into the phone, investigators traced and detained him and recovered the deceased’s mobile phone. The holster for the deceased’s pistol was found hanging from a tree along the same route where the body was found. It was possible that, like his mobile phone, the pistol was taken away by someone passing through the area. The officer said the deceased had suffered financial losses amounting to millions of rupees in investments, and he was supposed to return money invested by others. He added that Raza had asked one investor for a Rs30m loan because he was facing financial difficulties, but the request was declined. The alleged investor also told police that the deceased had told him he was having “weird thoughts”. His fiancée, in her statement to police, said that he was “obsessed” with his Bitcoin investment. She also told investigators that she had sent him a message late that night, but since he was already offline, he did not receive it. The officer said that despite all these developments, which strongly suggested the possibility of suicide, investigators still had three doubts. First, why did he travel to and choose that place in Gulistan-i-Jauhar? Secondly, his pistol has not been recovered so far, though the holster has been recovered. Thirdly, doctors told police that the bullet had been fired into his chest from close range. Yet gunshot residue was not detected on his hands, which is normally found when someone takes their own life using a firearm. It was possible that, since the body was partially decomposed, the residue on his hands could no longer be detected. Another officer, who is also familiar with the probe, said that investigators were making sincere and intensive efforts under the supervision of senior police officers. The call record data (CRD) of the deceased, along with details of his family background and friends, was also being obtained. Analysis of the available CCTV footage was also underway. The officer said the investigation would produce the “best results within a very short time”. Published in Dawn, August 3rd, 2026

PM Shehbaz congratulates PML-N after party maintains lead in second phase of AJK polls. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif congratulated the PML-N’s leadership and successful candidates on Monday after unofficial results of the second phase of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir showed it had won 14 of 18 seats up for grabs the previous day. The PML-N’s main rival in the contest and also its ally in the Centre, the PPP, has accused the PML-N of electoral malpractices, rigging and violence during Sunday polls, as it had during the first phase of the elections in Mirpur division on July 27. The PML-N secured nine of the 13 seats in the first phase while the PPP won the remaining four. Elections in AJK are being held in three phases over security concerns, with polling having been held on seven seats of Muzaffarabad division and 12 refugee seats — the reserved seats for refugees from India-occupied Kashmir — on Sunday. In the third phase, elections will be held in 11 constituencies of Poonch division. ‘Results reflect people’s confidence in PML-N’s policies’ A statement released by the PM’s Office on Monday said the premier congratulated PML-N’s leadership and successful candidates after their win in the second phase. “The continuity of this success is a result of the hard work of PML-N President Nawaz Sharif and the entire PML-N team,” the statement quoted PM Shehbaz as saying According to the statement, the premier noted that Nawaz and the PML-N team had conducted a successful electoral campaign in AJK and the party’s success “reflects the confidence of the people of AJK in PML-N’s policies”. He said the development and prosperity of AJK and the welfare of its people remained PML-N’s top priority. PM Shehbaz added that political parties had actively participated in the second phase of the AJK elections, which he said would further strengthen the democratic process. Results breakdown Earlier, state broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported the unofficial results of Sunday’s elections, citing Chief Election Commissioner Justice (retd) Ghulam Mustafa Mughal’s press talk in Muzaffarabad. During the press briefing, he announced that the PML-N had won 14 seats and the PPP four, the report said. Unofficial results LA-34 bagged by PML-N’s Nasir Dar LA-35 bagged by PML-N’s Chaudhry Muhammad Ismail LA-36 bagged by PML-N’s Muhammad Ahsan Raza LA-37 bagged by PNL-N’s Maryam Javed LA-38 bagged by PML-N’s Zeeshah Ali LA-39 bagged by PML-N’s Raja Muhammad Siddique Khan LA-41 bagged by PML-N’s Muhammad Amir Shah LA-42 bagged by PML-N’s Syed Shawkat Ali Shah LA-43 bagged by PML-N’s Muhammad Yasin Lone LA-44 bagged by PML-N’s Ahmad Raza Qadiri LA-25 bagged by PML-N’s Ghulam Qadir LA-30 bagged by PML-N’s Mustafa Bashir Abbasi LA-31 bagged by PML-N’s Saqib Majeed Khan LA-32 bagged by PML-N’s Raja Farooq Haider Khan LA-40 bagged by PPP’s Amir Abdul Ghaffar Khan LA-45 bagged by PPP’s Abdul Majid Khan LA-26 bagged by PPP’s Mian Abdul Waheed Khan LA-29 bagged by PPP’s Sardar Mukhtar Ahmad Khan Polling was postponed until Tuesday in LA-27 Muzaffarabad-I (Kutla) and at 71 of the 174 polling stations in LA-28 Muzaffarabad-II (Lachhrat) as polling staff and election material could not reach the constituency because of landslides and bad weather that resulted in blocked roads. PML-N now has ‘simple majority’ to form govt: Rana Sana As the unofficial results were released, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs and PML-N leader Rana Sanaullah said his party had now gained the “simple majority” needed to form a government in AJK. He was addressing a press conference alongside Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam. “We have the government-forming number,” he said, adding that “there are a total of 45 seats […] and out of 45, PML-N has so far secured 23 seats”. The PML-N leader said his party had won in four of the seven territorial constituencies in Muzaffarabad while the PPP, which had been “attempting to build a rigging narrative since 10:30am yesterday”, had secured three. Sanaullah demanded that the PPP must tell the people how they managed to secure three seats despite the alleged rigging. “Did they succeed because of rigging or because of a free and fair election?” Sanaullah further stated that the PML-N had also secured 10 out of 12 refugee seats while the PPP had won two. “A democratic government, which has the people’s mandate, will now be formed in AJK, and it will work on ideological, economic, and political affairs of the region,” he said. He added that a parliamentary party session of the PML-N would be called after the conclusion of the third phase of the elections for future decisions. Speaking about PPP’s rigging allegations, the PML-N leader dismissed them and accused PPP of colluding with the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) to disrupt the election process in Muzaffarabad. “Anticipating PML-N’s win, PPP along with the action committee planned riots and [..] fired at the police personnel when they got there,” Sanaullah alleged. He claimed that the incident created an atmosphere of fear in the area, which led to a lower turnout. “We received at least 3,000 to 4,000 fewer votes due to this,” he claimed. On PPP’s allegations that an attempt had been made on its candidate AJK Legislative Assembly Speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar’s life, he accused the party of staging a “drama”. He also claimed that the PPP had refused to get Akbar’s medicolegal examination done. Sanaullah accused the PPP of employing “dirty tricks” to sabotage the electoral process, saying that the PPP’s actions violated the Charter of Democracy, in which the party leadership had agreed that they would not “malign each other’s mandate with such dirty tricks”. Replying to a question, he said the PPP had raised doubts over “high turnout” in constituencies where the PML-N’s candidate had won. “With the kind of societal system in place in AJK, it is certainly possible that if there are 300 people in a village, 290 might show up to vote,” he said. He asked the PPP to follow due process in case of complaints rather than “building a narrative and disrupting democracy and the election process”. Reports of violence During the polling on Sunday, attempts were reportedly made to disrupt polling in some neighbourhoods of Muzaffarabad, but voting continued in most areas. In LA-31, Muzaffa­rabad-V (Khawra), clashes between workers of the PML-N and PPP were reported in Union Council Katkair. The PPP alleged that one of its workers, Syed Mushtaq Shah, was killed in an attack by PML-N supporters. The PML-N rejected the allegation, claiming the man suffered a cardiac arrest following a scuffle between two groups. There was no independent confirmation of either claim. PPP candidate and Legislative Assembly Speaker Akbar also wrote to the AJK chief election commissioner, alleging security lapses, firing incidents, interference in polling, prevention of polling agents from entering polling stations and denial of voting rights. He also claimed there had been an attempt on his life in which Advocate Syed Mumtaz Hussain Naqvi was injured, and called for an investigation and legal action against those responsible. There was no immediate response from the Election Commission. Clashes between workers of the two major parties, some involving the use of firearms, were also reported from other areas, though no casualties were immediately reported. Low turnout outside AJK Outside AJK, Kashmiris voted for their candidates vying for refugee seats at polling stations set up in Chakwal, Jhelum, Rawalpindi, Islamabad, Sialkot, Narowal, Sargodha, Attock, Nawabshah, Hyderabad, Mohmand, Mansehra, Quetta, Dera Ghazi Khan, Peshawar, Sanghar, and Naushahro Feroze. Polling in these areas largely remained peaceful and recorded a low turnout. In Mohmand, not a single voter turned up at a station set up for the AJK polls. In Dera Ghazi Khan, a single registered female voter cast her ballot at the Govt Elementary School in Maumori, where a polling station had been established just for her. Out of 12 refugee seats, seven seats are in Punjab, one seat is in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, one seat (Jammu-VI) is divided between Pun­jab, Islamabad, and Khyber Pakhtun­khwa, one seat is divided between Sindh and Balo­chistan (Valley-I), and one seat (Jammu-I) is shared among refugees living in Balochistan, Punjab, and Sindh. Valley-V seat is divided between Punjab and Islamabad. Since early June, AJK has witnessed protests by the now-proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding the abolition of the 12 refugee seats in the AJK legislature. The protests have also been marred by violence .

Israel conveys 'comments, concerns' to US on Gaza plan, says version made public does not reflect its position. Israel has conveyed concerns to the United States on a Gaza plan hailed by President Donald Trump after Hamas said it had agreed on disarmament, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said on Monday. “ Israel has conveyed its comments and concerns on the proposed framework to our American counterparts. The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions,” Doron Spielman, spokesman for the prime minister’s office, told AFP . He alleged that Israeli intelligence had found that Hamas had been rearming and recruiting forces since a ceasefire announced by Trump in October, which has reduced the level of violence although Israel has kept up strikes. Hamas announced on Friday that it had agreed to the next stage of a deal that includes handing over weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing committee. Trump called the move a “major milestone” in efforts to end the devastating war and told reporters that Israel was “very happy” about the developments. But Netanyahu’s spokesman said that Hamas’s actions showed it was preparing for “further October 7-style massacres” and noted that the plan released by Trump’s Board of Peace called for Gaza to be “a deradicalised terror-free zone that does not pose a threat to its neighbours”. “That vision stands in direct contrast to the current reality and to Hamas’s stated intentions. The indispensable first step toward any lasting arrangement is the genuine, verifiable and irreversible demilitarisation of Hamas,” he said. “Anything short of full demilitarisation will leave Hamas with the capability to threaten Israel again.” An Israeli official, speaking on condition of anonymity, earlier said that Israel, which still controls most of the Gaza Strip, would not withdraw forces under the plan without verifying disarmament by Hamas. Israel kept up strikes after the Hamas announcement, with Palestinian authorities on Sunday reporting that Israeli attacks killed at least 13 people. In the first 1,000 days of Israel’s attacks on Gaza since Oct 7, 2023, over 73,000 Palestinians had been killed, according to Palestinian authorities.

Bulls in charge as PSX opens week by gaining 1,700 points during intraday trade. The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) opened the week in the green, gaining more than 1,700 points during intraday trade. At 11am, the benchmark KSE-100 index had gained 2273.78 points, from the previous close of 176,094.11 points. By 2:18pm, the index’s gains had dropped to 1781.72 points. The development came as global oil prices tumbled on Monday as Donald Trump said fresh talks with Iran will begin later in the day. Mettis Global, a web-based financial portal, said the positive momentum at PSX came as “investors took cues from easing geopolitical tensions after Trump called off a planned strike on Iran, reducing immediate concerns over a wider regional conflict”. Awais Ashraf, director of research at AKD Securities, said investor optimism extended the positive momentum from the previous week, driven by expectations of a swift agreement between the US and Iran. “Sentiment improved after the US president announced that talks with Iran would resume on Monday, without setting a deadline for reaching an agreement following the cessation of hostilities,” he said. Ashraf added that “the return of inflation to single digits in July, with the data due to be released today, would provide an additional catalyst for the market by strengthening expectations of monetary easing and further boosting investor confidence”. The KSE-100 index ended the first month of the current fiscal year lower. According to Topline Securities Ltd, the index closed July down 4,208 points or 2.3 per cent month-on-month as escalating US-Iran tensions pushed global crude oil prices higher, weighing on investor sentiment. Average daily traded volume during the month stood at 845 million shares, while average daily traded value was Rs37.5bn. Additional input from AFP

Iran denies negotiations with US after Trump announces talks. Iran said on Monday that no negotiations with the United States were currently being held despite US President Donald Trump announcing earlier that the two sides were set to begin parleys later today. “Iran is not currently holding talks with the United States and is now in discussions with Oman over a temporary safe route through the Strait of Hormuz,” Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a televised press conference. On Sunday, Trump said that new negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the country to pursue a deal to end the war entering its sixth month. Trump told reporters that the talks would cover the Strait of Hormuz and ultimately, the denuclearisation of Iran. Oil prices fell on Monday at the opening of Asian trade after Trump announced the new negotiations, with West Texas Intermediate dropping 4.7 per cent to $80.72 per barrel. Following a return to strikes last month, fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again. Trump had threatened to hit Iran “very hard” and was reportedly considering renewed attacks including against energy infrastructure, with US embassies across the region on alert. Trump pulled back from that threat on Saturday, saying the “parameters” of a deal were there. “Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, without providing details of the venue or participants in the talks. The US president said he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on the strikes, which he claimed would have been “the biggest attack since World War II”. Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike. The US president said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran’s nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, though Tehran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature. ‘Exchange of views’ Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament’s national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June. That agreement was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, though it did include provisions on Hormuz. “They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views,” Ghashghavi said. Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, “We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed.” Iran deal with Oman? Before the war, there was free passage for all vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, but Iran closed the strait during the war and now insists on retaining control and charging tolls, something the US rejects. That dispute sparked the return to strikes last month, as Tehran refused to let ships travel any route other than one which hugs the Iranian coast. On Sunday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Baqaei told state television that a deal was close with Oman, which sits on the other side of the strait, over a new route through it. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides—neither the northern route nor the southern route — but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said. He insisted though that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait. Baqaei reiterated this during his televised address on Monday, saying that reaching an agreement with Oman was not sufficient to reopen the strait as the situation would remain unchanged while US “aggression” continued. He elaborated that Iran had been discussing with Oman the creation of a new route through the Strait of Hormuz that would be one path with entry and exit lanes. The Strait of Hormuz has become a sticking point in the Washington-Tehran conflict, which began with the US and Israel launching strikes on Iran on February 28. Iran has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the start of the war, ​causing energy prices to rise and stoking broader inflation. Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through Hormuz had dropped sharply. On Sunday, a tanker off the coast of Oman reported hearing an explosion near the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported, adding that the vessel and crew were all safe.

PH disputes China's claim of Scarborough combat drills, says reports ‘not credible’. The national government on Monday, Aug. 3, rejected China’s announcement that it carried out joint naval and air combat exercises around Bajo de Masinloc or Scarbororugh Shoal (Panatag Shoal) in the West Philippine Sea (WPS), saying available monitoring by security agencies did not support the claim. National Maritime Council (NMC) spokesperson Undersecretary Alexander Lopez said reports from the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) showed the continued presence of Chinese vessels in the area but did not detect the activities described by China. “Based on currently available reporting, the report that China conducted a joint naval-air combat patrol around Bajo de Masinloc on Aug. 1, 2026 was deemed not credible,” said Lopez, a retired admiral. “As per monitoring and reports from our AFP and PCG units, there is a presence of China Coast Guard, maritime militia, and People's Liberation Army-Navy (PLA-N) vessels at Bajo de Masinloc, as monitored and reported on a daily basis,” he continued. “But as to the actual conduct of navy-air combat drills, there were no such activities. This is again Chinese propaganda to ‘assert’ their maritime claims and support their activities over Bajo de Masinloc,” he added. 'Drills can't alter facts' The People's Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command announced on Aug. 1 that it had conducted joint naval and air exercises in and around Scarborough Shoal, known locally as Bajo de Masinloc, located 124 nautical miles from the coast of Zambales, within the 200 nautical mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of the country, and about 472 nautical miles from Hainan, the nearest point in China. Chinese state media reported that the drills involved H-6K bombers armed with YJ-12 supersonic anti-ship missiles, guided missile frigates, helicopters, amphibious vessels, and China Coast Guard ships carrying out interception, boarding, inspection, and towing operations. China announced the exercises days after Manila submitted to the United Nations (UN) its bid to extend its continental shelf beyond the country's 200-nautical-mile EEZ off Palawan. The national government also deposited its official nautical chart of Bajo de Masinloc with the UN. Beijing rejected both moves, describing them as illegal and insisting on its claim over the disputed shoal. It also urged the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf not to act on the Philippine submission. Despite China's statements, Lopez said military activities cannot change ownership or maritime entitlements under international law. “Be that as it may, even if China does conduct naval and air patrols around Bajo de Masinloc, such activities do not alter the legal status of the area, based on international law, including UNCLOS [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the 2016 Arbitral Award. Bajo de Masinloc remains an integral part of Philippine territory and the Philippines exercises sovereignty and sovereign rights over the maritime zones that surround it,” he said. “It is important to note that military drills cannot create sovereignty or maritime rights under international law,” he added. Continuous monitoring The NMC said the government will continue monitoring developments in the area while considering diplomatic action based only on verified information. “Any military drills at Bajo de Masinloc are deemed illegal and can pose security and safety issues to civilian shipping, air traffic, and fishing activities in the area. Diplomatic actions will be based on verified reports coming from our operational units, including the AFP, PCG, and BFAR [Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources],” Lopez said. Scarborough Shoal has remained one of the main flashpoints in the South China Sea, with repeated confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels. The dispute continues despite the 2016 arbitral ruling that invalidated China's sweeping claims in the South China Sea, a decision Beijing continues to reject.

Religious leader killed in Agusan del Sur ambush. BUTUAN CITY – A religious leader was killed and a tribal member was wounded in an ambush in Barangay Rizal, San Francisco, Agusan del Sur on Friday afternoon, July 31. Police identified the fatality as Pastor Balvino Andaya, 61, a leader of the Risen Christ Community Church, and the wounded as Avelino Cajandig, 59, a member of the Banwaon Manobo Talaandig Tribal Council (BAMATA-TC). Investigation said the victims were traveling aboard a Mitsubishi Montero Sport from Barangay Del Monte, Talacogon, Agusan del Sur when two unidentified motorcycle-riding suspects opened fire at their vehicle. The Sports Utility Vehicle veered off the road and crashed into a roadside sari-sari store. The Police Regional Office-13 on Monday ordered an extensive investigation of the incident and manhunt against the suspects. A case conference was held at the San Francisco Municipal Police Station (MPS) led by PRO-13 Director Police Brig. Gen. Marcial Mariano P. Magistrado IV where investigators presented updates on the circumstances surrounding the incident, evidence gathered, intelligence developments, and the progress of ongoing investigative and follow-up operations. Andaya died from multiple bullet wounds. Cajandig sustained a bullet wound and being treated in an undisclosed hospital. Recovered from the area were several fired cartridge cases and fired bullets. These pieces of evidence were submitted for forensic and ballistic examinations PRO-13 Public Information Office chief Police Lt. Col. Jennifer S. Ometer said hot-pursuit and follow-up operations are in full swing. “Our ground personnel are in round-the-clock operation to solve this incident,” Ometer added. Magistrado activated “Oplan: Cure” to further strengthen operational support and sustain the manhunt for the perpetrators. “We assure the public that PRO-13 is exhausting all available investigative and intelligence resources to ensure the immediate identification and arrest of those responsible for this senseless act of violence,” Magistrado said. “We also call on anyone with information that may aid the investigation to immediately coordinate with the nearest police station. Together, we can ensure that those responsible are held fully accountable under the law.” Ometer said PRO-13 remains steadfast in its commitment to delivering swift, impartial, and thorough investigations while upholding the rule of law and ensuring the safety and security of every community in the Caraga region.

Senators slam TRO on P85 daily minimum wage hike implementation. Senators on Monday, August 3 criticized the issuance of a temporary restraining order issued by a Pasig City Regional Trial Court against the implementation of the P85 daily minimum wage increase in Metro Manila. The petition filed by Readycon Trading and Construction Corp. and R-11 Builders, Inc. before Pasig RTC Branch 152 sought to stop the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board—NCR and the National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC) from implementing the expected wage increase until August 13. Sen. Raffy Tulfo pointed out that the court’s action is unacceptable since Article 126 of the Labor Code clearly states that no court, tribunal or other authority may issue a preliminary injunction, permanent injunction, or TRO against any hearing, action or proceeding of the Regional Wage Boards. Tulfo argued that an appeal should have gone through the proper process and been filed with the appropriate agency, which in this case, should have been the NWPC. “The wage increase is already meager dspite the continuous rise in the prices of goods, and now even that has been denied to our struggling workers who simply want to make ends meet,” Tulfo said in a statement. It may be recalled that the additional P85 in the daily minimum wage was divided into two phases—the P60, which took effect on July 25, while the remaining P25 increase will be implemented starting January 1, 2027.Tulfo lamented that the court’s action was a major blow to the livelihoods of Filipino workers. “Suspending their wage increase is an even greater violation of theri rights, especially amid the continuing rise in the prices of basic goods. The lives and livelihoods of laborerrs should take precedence in this matter,” he said. “The court should no longer interfere in this issue, and it would be better for these companies—who show no appreciation for the contributions of their workers to their businesses—to pursue their appeal through the proper process,” the senator said. Tulfo said he will soon file a bill to amend the provisions of Article 126 of the Labor Code so that there would no longer be confusion in the implementation of the law regarding wage hikes. Sen. Risa Hontiveros also lamented the decision of the court, pointing out that there are already solutions on the table that can be implemented by the government at this point in time. “First, the P85 wage hike must be implemented. It’s already a modest increase, and it’s even being paid in installments. Groups such as the Financial Executives Institute of the Philippines have already agreed to it, and some employers are prepared to provide the wage increase. So workers should not lose this pay raise simply because it has been blocked in court,” Hontiveros said. She said the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) should fight the case so it can be dismissed as possible, or so the suspension of the wage hike can be lifted. “I also urge our business community: let us go through the administrative processes for exemption. Let us respect the law and the tripartite system in which workers, employers, and the government all have a voice,” she appealed. “If this system is bypassed, the predictability and industrial peace that allow businesses to thrive will be put at risk,” she stressed. Hontiveros also said that alongside higher wages, the government should pursue the lowering of electricity costs. She pointed out the government cannot give workers a wage increase with one hand only to take it back through higher electricity bills with the other. “When it comes to the wage hike and reducing electricity charges, we have solutions, we have the means, and we can fix this,” she said. Sen. Joel Villanueva, chairman of the Senate Committee on Labor and Employment said that while he respects the court’s decision he is confused by the ruling. Villanueva also cited the inacceptability of the TRO, citing Article 126 of the Labor Code. “As head of the Senate labor panel, I’m also saddened by this development. This increase is badly needed by our workers. I’m also confused by that decision primarily because of Article 126 of the Labor Code,” he said. “I’m more than willing to be corrected, but that is also my understanding of the law," added Villanueva. Nevertheless, Villanueva said he hope and pray that the matter be soon resolved and any legal questions regarding the wage increase would be clarified.
